concept.name: Overconfidence bias
concept.definition: A cognitive bias in which subjective confidence in one's judgments reliably exceeds their objective accuracy, appearing as overestimation of one's own performance, overplacement relative to others, or overprecision of beliefs. In markets it is linked empirically to excessive trading volume and to the underperformance of the most active individual traders.
concept.intuition: Traders systematically think their forecasts are better than they are - when they say 90% sure, they are right far less than 90% of the time.
concept.mechanics: Measured by calibration studies (confidence versus hit rate), better-than-average surveys, and confidence-interval tasks in which 90% intervals capture the truth only about half the time. Barber and Odean linked overconfidence to trading frequency and showed that the most active individual investors earned the lowest net returns.
concept.failure_modes: Overplacement reverses on hard tasks (people then rate themselves below average), and some better-than-average findings reflect event base rates rather than bias. Experts in high-validity environments with rapid feedback can be well calibrated, so the bias is context-dependent.
concept.misconceptions: Overconfidence is not simply optimism or high self-esteem; it is a calibration error between confidence and accuracy. Nor is more information a cure - in Oskamp's study confidence rose with information while accuracy stayed flat.
concept.example: Barber and Odean (2000, summarized in the SEC-commissioned LOC report) found that the most actively trading individual investors underperformed the market, consistent with overconfidence-driven overtrading.

citations.source: Behavioral Patterns and Pitfalls of U.S. Investors (Library of Congress, Federal Research Division, prepared for the U.S. SEC, August 2010)
citations.section: Overconfidence section, p. 3; Active Trading section, pp. 7-8
